data.name: Doorways: The Underworld
data.detailed_description:
Doorways: The Underworld is a first person horror adventure, featuring a complex story and deep atmosphere. It will challenge you with its fast-paced gameplay and breathtaking visuals and sounds, so prepare to immerse yourself in a terrifying psychological experience.

The Underworld is the third chapter of Doorways. It is not necessary to have the first chapters in order to play this game. But we recommend to do so for a better understand of the story.

You're playing as Thomas Foster, a special agent who must track a missing psychopath. Who is she? What is this place and how did you get here?

These are just some of the questions that you must answer during your journey...

Key Features


  • Horrifying exploration adventure with an immersive atmosphere
  • Ingenious puzzles as well as challenges that put your reflexes at test
  • Inspired voice acting by Sam A. Mowry (the voice of Alexander in Amnesia: The Dark Descent)
  • Replayability through many secret places
  • Full Controller support
  • Native Oculus Rift support

----

Doorways is an episodic game, it's divided in three parts and they can be played separately:

Doorways: Prelude (Chapter 1 & 2):


Doorways: The Underworld (Chapter 3):


Doorways: Holy Mountains of Flesh (Chapter 4):


----

IMPORTANT
Achievements do not work on Linux

reviews.review:
Doorways: The Underworld is the second game in the franchise, and contains the third chapter of the series. Despite being technically a "third chapter", I would consider this to be its own standalone game rather than a continuation of the first, because you don't necessarily have to play the first game to have any real understanding of what is going on in this one. Quite frankly they feel disconnected both in tone, and in story. 

This was a much better and more cohesive game than the first one (Doorways: Prelude). Even though I did enjoy that game for what it was, it was little more than a walking simulator with some very un-scary jump scares thrown in the mix. The main difference between this game and the first one is that in each section of this game, there is a different monster that is hunting you, which you have to avoid, and hide from. This is the one major difference that makes this feel more like a "game" and less like a "walking simulator"; there is an actual condition in which you can "lose" (the monster catches you) and a condition by which you can "win" (you escape without the monster catching you). It's so simple, but it makes the game actually feel like a game.  This game is quite a bit scarier than the first. While I never audibly screamed, I did feel incredibly uneasy and tense during certain portions, but I won't spoil anything. As opposed to the first, it feels like a proper horror game.

The story of the first game was hard to follow, both in chapters 1 and 2, and both of those stories felt less interesting and just overall more pointless and confusing. I would say they were teetering on being somewhat pretentious (especially chapter 2). It's also longer, not in total runtime, but there are three distinct sections that you play though, which total out to be about the same length as the first game when summed together, but they're all part of chapter three and are connected to the same story. The third chapter of this game, starting in the hospital, I would consider to be the highlight of the game. It was particularly good, and I enjoyed it quite a bit. It was very atmospheric and nightmarish, and made me feel very isolated and claustrophobic. There is a mechanic in the third act of the game which you might recognize if you played Titanfall: 2, which was really cool to see. I'm glad they added that in, it made the game a lot more interesting.

I think that I would recommend this game to anyone who likes indie horror games. The story felt a lot more fleshed out and complete than either chapters one or two, and the gameplay was a lot better. By modern standards this game might be a bit dated; it has been sitting in my Steam library for over a decade, but I am glad that I played it, and I will be adding part 3 to my Wishlist. 

One thing that I do want to point out: there was a game-breaking bug in the third act of the game where I got crushed by two walls that collapsed in on me as I was pulling a lever. Instead of just dying, my character became stuck, and I could not move, I could not die, and I could not even pause the game. When I alt+f4, I reloaded into the game, and I had lost all of the progress on that section. Not a huge deal, but, it did make me waste about five minutes of my time. Not that I'm asking for a 12 year old game to be patched or anything, but still. It was a bit jank. There was also one part of chapter three where you have to put a certain item on top of another certain thing in order to get access to a key. It was quite difficult to tell where I was supposed to find that "thing", and I spent a few minutes running around confused before I figured it out. I'm not one to ask for "yellow paint" in my games, but, that one particular point of the game was definitely not clear to me in terms of what I was supposed to do. A bit of a head scratcher. 

Is this game worth $10.00? Probably, but, that's debatable. I guess it depends on who you ask. This game is about the length of a movie, and I enjoyed it, and ten bucks is about the same price as a movie ticket, so, in my opinion, I would say ten for this is a fair price, but, if you can get it on sale, then you definitely should. I'm quite surprised to see that less than 10% of the players who bought this game and played it actually made it to the end of the game, however, it is a horror game, so maybe you guys are just a bunch of wusses.
